## DI-0301 reaches the instrument it's been circling since module 3

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is back, and this time she's holding the thread last module
deliberately left dangling: Lakeshore's aging stand-alone laboratory instrument, tagged in the
equipment log as **Asset LAB-07** — a benchtop analyzer older than Part 11 itself. It's never been
replaced. Nobody's ever formally asked whether it still gets to be treated the way it always has.

LAB-07 earns its keep quietly. Every morning, before the day's blood-typing reagents go anywhere
near a donor or patient sample, a lab tech runs a quality-control (QC) check on them through LAB-07:
a small reagent sample goes in, the instrument reads it, and a thermal-paper strip prints out a
single number — an absorbance reading — next to a pass or fail flag. The tech initials the strip,
dates it, and files it in the day's QC binder. That's been the routine since before BECS (Blood
Establishment Computer Software) existed, back when the whole lab recorded its QC checks by hand
into a logbook and LAB-07 was just the machine that gave you the number to write down.

DI-0301 — your QA's data-integrity self-assessment — has already resolved two threads: **DED-0458**
(module 1's BECS donor-eligibility record, now settled except for "accurate," still open) and
Fairview's paper donor file (module 3, settled as Fairview's own record of record). Last module
planted a question about LAB-07 and left it open on purpose: is this instrument more like the Food
and Drug Administration's (FDA's) own pH-meter example — a simple readout that genuinely *is* the
original record — or more like FDA's own FT-IR (Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy) example,
where the real record is an electronic trace that can be reprocessed, and a printout can quietly
leave something out?

Your QA found the answer isn't as simple as either one. While reading LAB-07's original manual —
something nobody at Lakeshore had opened in years — she found a second mode almost nobody knows
exists. No citations yet. Just the instrument, the manual, and the question she's bringing you.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure this module exists to head off: a piece of equipment that keeps producing
results nobody questions, year after year, purely because it's always worked — while the actual
question FDA would ask ("can you prove, on paper, that this thing is still fit for what you use it
for, and that its records are secure and trustworthy?") never gets asked by anyone at all. A system
can run flawlessly for decades and still be a compliance gap, because "it runs" and "someone can
prove it should still be trusted" are not the same fact.

You already run the discipline this needs, under a name you already know: **legacy system
management**, and the **technical debt** it accumulates. You already track which systems in your
environment are old enough that "it still runs" and "it's actually supportable and well-documented"
have quietly become two different claims. Problem management gives you the sharper version of the
same idea: the **root-cause-versus-symptom** distinction. "The system still works" is a symptom —
something you can observe by watching it run. Whether it's been kept in a genuinely documented,
defensible state is the deeper question a real problem record would actually need answered, and
watching it run never answers that question by itself.

Here's where the regulated world demands more. In ordinary IT operations, a legacy system that still
works is very often left alone indefinitely, on the honest logic of "if it ain't broke, don't touch
it" — nobody opens a problem ticket just because a stable system is old. For a Part 11 (21 CFR —
Code of Federal Regulations — Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures) legacy system,
"it still works" isn't the test at all.
FDA's own guidance sets a specific, four-part test instead, and one of those four parts demands
*documented evidence and justification* — on an ongoing basis — that the system is fit for its
intended use. Skip that documentation, and enforcement discretion simply stops applying, no matter
how reliably the instrument keeps printing results.

## The rule in plain English

A **legacy system**, for Part 11's purposes, isn't just "an old system." It's a specific, narrow
category: a system that was already up and running before Part 11's effective date — **August 20,
1997** — and that has kept meeting the rules that governed it ever since. FDA built a real,
four-part test around that category, and — this is the part worth
getting exactly right — passing it isn't automatic, and it isn't permanent. It isn't automatic
because every one of the four conditions has to actually be true, with evidence, not just assumed
because the system is old. It isn't permanent because the fourth condition asks for documented
justification on an ongoing basis, not a one-time pass stamped at installation and never revisited.
An instrument can lose its legacy-system status years after it first qualified, simply by nobody
keeping that documentation current.

This whole module sits at **guidance tier**: everything here comes from FDA's 2003 Part 11 guidance
(*Scope and Application*), the same source last module used for predicate rules and the
narrow-interpretation test. It's FDA's current thinking, written in "should" and "intend to" language
— not binding regulation. This module doesn't introduce a new regulation-tier citation beyond what's
already in this curriculum; the four-part test itself is an enforcement-discretion policy, not a CFR
section with its own number.

Sets the four-part test: FDA doesn't intend to enforce *any* Part 11 requirement against a system that meets all four criteria. | The test DI-0301 runs against LAB-07, criterion by criterion. |
| The same section's closing sentence | "the legacy-systems section's own closing line" | Guidance tier. If a legacy system has been changed since 1997 in a way that breaks predicate-rule compliance, Part 11 controls should apply going forward. | The question DI-0301 asks about LAB-07's service history — has anything about it ever actually changed? |
| FDA 2003 guidance, footnote 7 (defining "legacy system") | "footnote seven" | Guidance tier. Defines the term itself: "we use the term legacy system to describe systems already in operation before the effective date of part 11." | Confirms LAB-07 fits the category this test was written for. |
| FDA 2003 guidance, § III.C.4, "Copies of Records" | "section three-C-four, copies of records" | Guidance tier. Enforcement discretion on specific §11.10(b) copy-generation requirements; all records remain subject to inspection under predicate rules; recommends common portable or converted formats for copies. | What format DI-0301 should expect LAB-07 to hand an inspector, and whether LAB-07 can actually produce it. |

One of §11.10's closed-system controls: the ability to generate accurate, complete copies of records. | The specific requirement the "Copies of Records" section's enforcement discretion attaches to — named for context, not developed further here. |

## The actual text

Start with the four-part test itself, quoted verbatim from
`sources/fda-guidance/part-11-scope-and-application-2003.md`, § III.C.3, "Legacy Systems":

> This means that the Agency does not intend to take enforcement action to enforce compliance with
> any part 11 requirements if all the following criteria are met for a specific system:
>
> - The system was operational before the effective date.
> - The system met all applicable predicate rule requirements before the effective date.
> - The system currently meets all applicable predicate rule requirements.
> - You have documented evidence and justification that the system is fit for its intended use
>   (including having an acceptable level of record security and integrity, if applicable).

Read that word "all" twice. Not three of four. Not "mostly." All four, or the enforcement-discretion
umbrella FDA describes for legacy systems doesn't cover the system at all.

Now the sentence that keeps this from being a one-time pass, quoted in full, from the same section:

> If a system has been changed since August 20, 1997, and if the changes would prevent the system
> from meeting predicate rule requirements, Part 11 controls should be applied to Part 11 records
> and signatures pursuant to the enforcement policy expressed in this guidance.

And the guidance's own definition of the term, quoted from its footnote 7:

> In this guidance document, we use the term legacy system to describe systems already in operation
> before the effective date of part 11.

### Running the four-part test against LAB-07

Here's DI-0301's actual exercise — the same criterion-by-criterion discipline module 3 used for the
pH-meter-versus-FT-IR question, now applied to a real piece of Lakeshore equipment.

**Criterion 1 — operational before August 20, 1997. Clean yes.** Lakeshore's own equipment file
still holds LAB-07's original installation record: a purchase order and an asset-tagging entry,
both dated years before Part 11's effective date, plus early logbook pages in the same lab notebook
that show LAB-07's QC results being recorded by hand, long before BECS existed. This is the easiest
of the four to confirm, and it's worth noticing exactly why it's easy: it's a historical fact backed
by a surviving paper trail, not an assumption resting on "it feels old."

**Criterion 2 — met all applicable predicate rule requirements before the effective date. Yes,
supportable.** Those same retained logbook pages show LAB-07's QC results being documented the way
the lab's own procedure at the time required: a reading, a pass/fail call, an initial, a date. That's
thin evidence compared to criterion 1's purchase order, but it's real evidence, not silence — the
logbook itself is the artifact that answers this criterion.

**Criterion 3 — currently meets all applicable predicate rule requirements. Yes, and this is where
the changed-system sentence actually gets used, not just quoted.** Your QA asks the sharp, concrete
question the guidance's closing sentence demands: has LAB-07 ever been patched, had its firmware
updated, or had any component replaced since 1997? The honest answer: its thermal print mechanism has
been swapped twice over the years, by a vendor technician under a standard service contract, each
time logged in the maintenance file. Its underlying measurement method and embedded software have
never been touched. Applying the test exactly as written: did either repair *prevent the system from
meeting predicate rule requirements*? No — the lab's QC procedure still gets satisfied the same way
it always has, with the same measurement logic, just a replacement part doing the printing. A worn
print head failing and getting swapped isn't the kind of change the guidance is warning about. This
criterion holds, and it holds for a documented, reasoned reason — not because nobody asked the
question.

**Criterion 4 — documented evidence and justification that the system is fit for its intended use,
including acceptable record security and integrity. Genuinely uncertain — and this is DI-0301's real
finding.** Your QA went looking for the actual artifact this criterion asks for: a document — a
memo, a periodic equipment review, anything — that states, on the record, that LAB-07 is still fit
for its intended use and that its records are adequately secure and intact. She couldn't find one.
Not a wrong document. No document. What she found instead is daily proof that LAB-07 *functions*:
QC checks pass every morning, the printout comes out, nobody's filed a complaint about it in living
memory. That's real, and it matters — but it isn't the same claim the test actually requires. "It
still works" is something you can observe by watching it run. "There is documented evidence and
justification that it's fit for its intended use, including an acceptable level of record security
and integrity" is a specific, written artifact the test asks you to produce. Lakeshore has the first.
It doesn't yet have the second.

This is not a confirmed violation, and it shouldn't be treated like one. Nothing here proves LAB-07
is unfit, insecure, or non-compliant. The finding is a gap in *evidence*, not a proven failure — the
same honest distinction this curriculum has drawn before (module 1's "accurate" on DED-0458, module
2's audit-trail review frequency). The right response isn't to panic, and it isn't to replace the
instrument. It's to go get, or create, the documentation the test actually asks for: a short,
dated qualification review — someone with the authority to say so, confirming LAB-07 still performs
its intended function, that its printed QC records haven't been shown to be tampered with or lost,
and that the lab's handling of those printouts (initialed, dated, filed) is adequate. That's a
findable, fixable gap, not a five-alarm fire.

### Resolving the pH-meter-versus-FT-IR question for LAB-07

Last module planted this exactly, and quoted FDA's own contrast in full (Question 10 of the 2018
data-integrity guidance): a pH meter or balance that produces a paper printout *as* the original
record satisfies retention once that printout is kept; an instrument like FT-IR, whose underlying
electronic record is genuinely dynamic — reprocessable, re-baselined — loses real information if only
a static printout is kept, and FDA's own example warns a printout might not even show the full
spectrum, potentially excluding contaminants from view. Module 3 built that distinction; this module
applies it, one piece of actual equipment at a time, rather than re-deriving it.

For its ordinary, everyday path, **LAB-07 is the pH-meter case.** The QC check a tech runs every
morning produces exactly one output: a single absorbance number and a pass/fail flag, printed once,
on the spot. There's no underlying file behind that printout that anyone queries, re-sorts, or
reprocesses — the printed strip, initialed and filed, genuinely *is* the whole record of that check.
Nothing is lost by keeping the strip. That's precisely FDA's pH-meter logic, applied honestly, not
assumed because the instrument is old.

Here's the twist your QA actually found, reading the manual nobody else had opened in years: **LAB-07
has a second mode nobody uses, and that mode is FT-IR-like, not pH-meter-like.** Buried in its original
documentation is a data-export function — built for a connected workstation this lab stopped using
long ago — that can save the instrument's full absorbance scan across the whole wavelength range as a
trace file, not just the single summary number the daily printout shows. That trace file can be
reopened and reprocessed: a different baseline applied, the curve re-smoothed, the result recalculated
from the raw scan. Nobody at Lakeshore has used that mode in years. Nobody realized it still existed.
But it's still physically present on the instrument, and nothing in writing says it's off-limits.

That matters, because it means LAB-07 isn't a clean, single-case answer. It's a **split finding**,
and that's the honest one: the instrument's actual, relied-upon daily output is a static printout that
genuinely is the original record — the pH-meter case, settled. But its dormant export/reprocessing
mode, if anyone ever switched it on, would produce a genuinely dynamic electronic record — the
FT-IR case — and a printout taken from *that* mode would be a frozen snapshot of something built to
be examined more than one way, the same risk FDA's own example warns about. The fix isn't technical.
It's documentation, using the same tool module 3 already built: write down, in LAB-07's own QC
procedure, that the daily absorbance printout is the relied-upon record of record, and that the
export/reprocessing mode is either formally prohibited for QC determinations or — if anyone ever
has a reason to use it — treated from that point forward as producing a dynamic record subject to its
own review and retention requirements, not casually swapped in as "the" result because it happened to
be convenient that day. Static versus dynamic, and the narrow-interpretation reliance test — what
you actually rely on to do the regulated work — is module 3's framework; this is that same framework,
now pointed at a specific piece of lab equipment instead of a database record.

### Copies of records — what LAB-07 hands an inspector

FDA's 2003 guidance also addresses copies directly, quoted in full from the same source, § III.C.4,
"Copies of Records":

> The Agency intends to exercise enforcement discretion with regard to specific part 11 requirements
> for generating copies of records (§ 11.10 (b) and any corresponding requirement in §11.30). You
> should provide an investigator with reasonable and useful access to records during an inspection.
> All records held by you are subject to inspection in accordance with predicate rules (e.g., §§
> 211.180(c), (d), and 108.35(c)(3)(ii)).
>
> We recommend that you supply copies of electronic records by:
>
> - Producing copies of records held in common portable formats when records are maintained in these
>   formats
> - Using established automated conversion or export methods, where available, to make copies in a
>   more common format (examples of such formats include, but are not limited to, PDF, XML, or SGML)

Two things at once, and both matter: enforcement discretion applies to the *specific generating-copies
mechanics* of §11.10(b) itself — but every record LAB-07 produces is still fully subject to inspection
under the predicate rule, full stop. FDA isn't saying inspectors get less access. It's saying the
precise technical method of producing a copy isn't what FDA intends to police line-by-line.

Applied to LAB-07, practically: for the ordinary daily QC printout, the answer is easy. The printout
*is* the original record, so a clean photocopy or scan of it — ideally a scanned PDF, since thermal
paper fades over time, which is its own separate retention concern this course's next module picks
up — preserves its content and meaning exactly. That satisfies the guidance's recommendation without
any special effort: a "common portable format," produced by an "established... conversion... method,"
with nothing lost in translation.

The export/reprocessing mode is where LAB-07 actually falls short, and it's worth flagging now, before
an inspector ever asks. If that mode were ever used, its only output is a raw trace file in an old,
instrument-specific format — tied to companion software built for a workstation this lab no longer
operates. There's no built-in conversion to PDF, XML, or anything else an inspector could read without
that same obsolete software. Right now, that gap is dormant: the mode isn't used, so the gap isn't
live. But it's exactly the kind of thing DI-0301 is supposed to surface before it becomes a real
problem — a capability sitting on the instrument that, if anyone ever switched it on, Lakeshore
currently has no good way to hand over in a format the guidance actually recommends.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessor
wouldn't ask whether Lakeshore has a legacy-system policy. They'd ask for the specific artifact each
criterion of the four-part test actually requires.

**For criteria 1 and 2:** the purchase and installation record, and the earliest logbook pages
showing QC results documented under the procedure of the time — exactly the paper trail DI-0301
already found. A bad answer sounds like "it's been here forever." A good answer produces the
documents.

**For criterion 3:** the maintenance and service log — every repair, part swap, or software touch
LAB-07 has had since 1997, with a clear statement of whether any of them affected its measurement
method or its ability to meet the predicate rule. A bad answer sounds like "nothing's really
changed." A good answer names each change and explains, specifically, why it didn't matter.

**For criterion 4:** a dated qualification or fitness-for-use review — the exact document DI-0301
couldn't find. A bad answer sounds like "it's never given us a problem." A good answer points to a
specific memo or review, signed by someone with the authority to make that call, addressing both
function *and* record security and integrity.

QSE 3 (Equipment), one of AABB's Quality System Essentials, is the adjacent drawer here — equipment
qualification and fitness-for-use documentation generally, paraphrased only, no specific standard
number developed in this module.

## Common traps

**"It still works, so it's fine."** This is the trap this module exists to refute, and LAB-07's own
criterion 4 is the refutation, built in. FDA's four-part test doesn't ask whether a system functions
— it asks for documented evidence and justification that it's fit for its intended use, including
record security and integrity. A system can run perfectly, every day, for years, and still fail this
specific requirement, because "it runs" and "someone can produce the documentation proving it should
still be trusted" are two different claims. Only the second one is what the test actually requires.

**"Once a system qualifies as a legacy system, it's grandfathered forever."** Not quite. The test's
own fourth criterion demands evidence on an ongoing basis, not a one-time pass stamped at some point
in the past. And the guidance's own closing sentence makes the point explicit: if a legacy system is
later changed in a way that breaks predicate-rule compliance, Part 11 controls apply going forward —
the legacy status isn't a permanent exemption, it's a conditional one, re-earned by staying true,
continuously, not granted once and forgotten.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask whether anyone can produce LAB-07's — or any legacy system's — documented fitness-for-use
  justification, by name.** "It's never given us trouble" is not that document. A dated review with
  someone's name on it is.
- **Treat a missing criterion-4 document as an actionable gap to fix, not a reason to panic or
  replace the equipment.** The fix is usually a short, honest qualification memo — not a capital
  project.
- **Ask what's changed on any legacy system since it was installed — parts, firmware, software —
  and whether each change was actually assessed against predicate-rule requirements**, the way
  LAB-07's print-head swaps were. Don't let "nothing's really changed" stand in for an actual answer.
- **Find out whether a legacy instrument has a mode nobody uses, and ask what it would produce if
  someone did.** LAB-07's export function was sitting there, unused and unassessed, until DI-0301
  went looking. A dormant capability is still a capability.
- **Before an inspection, confirm what format a copy of each legacy system's records would actually
  take, and whether the system can produce it.** A clean scan of a paper printout is usually fine. A
  proprietary export file nobody can open without obsolete software usually isn't — and that's worth
  knowing before an investigator asks, not after.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA reports, "LAB-07 passes every QC check every morning, and nobody's ever complained about it — so criterion 4 of the legacy-system test is satisfied." Is she right?

No — and this is the central nuance this module exists to teach. Criterion 4 of FDA's four-part test
doesn't ask whether a system functions day to day. It asks for *documented evidence and justification*
that the system is fit for its intended use, including an acceptable level of record security and
integrity. "It passes every morning" is evidence the instrument works. It is not the same thing as a
dated review, signed by someone with the authority to make the call, stating that LAB-07 is fit for
its intended use and that its records are adequately secure. Lakeshore has the first. Until someone
produces the second, criterion 4 is a genuine open gap — not a proven violation, but not satisfied
either.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: LAB-07's thermal print mechanism has been replaced twice since Part 11 took effect. Does that automatically reopen the whole four-part legacy-system test?

Not automatically — you have to actually ask the question the guidance's own closing sentence asks:
did the change prevent the system from meeting predicate rule requirements? Here, it didn't. The
print-head swaps replaced a worn part under a standard service arrangement; LAB-07's underlying
measurement method and embedded software were untouched, and the lab's QC documentation requirement
is still met exactly as it was before. Criterion 3 — "currently meets all applicable predicate rule
requirements" — holds, and it holds for a reasoned, documented reason. A different kind of change —
say, a firmware update that altered how a result gets calculated — would need the same question
asked just as seriously, and might come out the other way.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Must Lakeshore hand an inspector LAB-07's records specifically as a PDF file, because that's what FDA's guidance requires?

No — and this is **not a regulatory requirement** read correctly. FDA's 2003 guidance's "Copies of
Records" section is guidance tier, "we recommend" language, not a regulation mandating one specific
file format. It recommends common portable formats, or established conversion/export methods, with
PDF, XML, and SGML named only as *examples*. The real, binding piece underneath it is the predicate
rule: every record stays subject to inspection, and a copy has to preserve its content and meaning.
For LAB-07's daily printout, a scanned PDF is a sensible, easy way to meet that recommendation — but
the requirement is "preserve content and meaning in a reasonably accessible format," not "must be a
PDF specifically."
:::

## Where this goes next

DI-0301 now has a real, worked answer for LAB-07: a clean pass on whether it's old enough and once
compliant enough to qualify as a legacy system, a reasoned pass on whether its service history still
keeps it compliant today, a genuine, fixable gap on the documented-justification criterion, and a
split, concrete answer to the pH-meter-versus-FT-IR question module 3 planted — simple daily printout,
dormant dynamic export mode, two different answers for two different outputs of the same instrument.
Next, `retention-across-record-types` goes beyond 606.160(d)'s product-record clock to ask what
"retain the record" actually requires once you know whether what you're retaining is static or
dynamic — the exact distinction this module just finished applying to LAB-07's own two output modes.
